column1: How do PARTITION BY and ORDER BY differ in a MergeTree table?
column2: They are orthogonal. PARTITION BY physically splits the table into separate on-disk directories (one per partition value) and enables skipping whole directories; ORDER BY sorts rows within a part and builds the sparse primary index for finding rows inside data you've decided to read.

Skipping entire partitions before reading any granule, using partition/MinMax metadata, when the query's WHERE filters on the partition key. In EXPLAIN indexes=1 it shows as Parts dropping (e.g. 36/36 to 3/36) at the MinMax/Partition stage.

column1: Why is a coarse partition key like toYYYYMM preferred over a high-cardinality one?
column2: Every partition is at least one part, so partitioning by something high-cardinality (user_id, toStartOfMinute) explodes the part count and triggers TOO_MANY_PARTS. Aim for tens-to-low-hundreds of partitions, typically a monthly or daily date bucket.

column1: Can a single part span two partitions?
column2: No. A part belongs to exactly one partition; that is what makes DROP PARTITION and TTL cheap metadata operations instead of row-by-row deletes.

column1: When does the partition key help a query, and when is it dead weight?
column2: It helps only when the query filters on the partition key (pruning). Partition on month but query by user_id with no date filter and you pay partitioning overhead for zero pruning benefit.

column1: Why can a point lookup in ClickHouse read ~90K rows to return ~30 matching rows?
column2: The sparse primary index skips at granule granularity (~8192 rows/mark), not row granularity. It guarantees reading only matching granules, never only matching rows, so it reads whole granules around the matches.

column1: In EXPLAIN indexes=1, what does binary search vs generic exclusion search tell you?
column2: binary search means the filter hit the ORDER BY prefix (leading key column) and the PK can jump directly. generic exclusion search means the filter is on a non-prefix key column, so the PK can only exclude some granules and it's slower.

column1: Two tables, same data, WHERE user_id=42: ORDER BY (user_id,event_date) reads 90K rows, ORDER BY (country,event_date,user_id) reads 957K. Why?
column2: When user_id is the leading key, binary search jumps to its granules. When user_id is last, granules are sorted by country then event_date, so almost every granule's user_id min/max spans a range including 42 and can't be skipped, forcing a near-scan.

column1: What is the practical rule for ordering columns in ORDER BY?
column2: Put the highest-selectivity / most-frequently-filtered column first; the leading column gets true binary-search skipping, trailing columns get much weaker skipping.

column1: What is the index funnel shown by EXPLAIN indexes=1, in order?
column2: MinMax then Partition then PrimaryKey. Each stage reports Parts and Granules selected out of total, and each narrows what the next stage sees (e.g. MinMax/Partition drop whole parts, PrimaryKey drops granules within survivors).

column1: Dense vs sparse primary index: Postgres B-tree vs ClickHouse MergeTree?
column2: Postgres B-tree is dense: one entry per row pointing at the exact tuple, so a filter resolves to exact rows (great for OLTP point lookups). ClickHouse is sparse: one entry per ~8192-row granule, so a filter resolves to granules (great for OLAP range scans, wasteful for single-row lookups).

column1: On a full-table sum(amount), why does Postgres read all columns but ClickHouse reads only one?
column2: Postgres is a row-store: a Seq Scan pulls whole rows (all columns) off disk even to sum one column. ClickHouse is a column-store: it reads only the amount column file. On wide tables this ratio is the core reason OLAP engines are columnar.

column1: How many physical sort orders does a ClickHouse MergeTree table have, and how do you serve other access patterns?
column2: Exactly one, defined by ORDER BY. Any other access pattern is a scan unless you add a data-skipping index or a projection; contrast Postgres, where you can add many independent secondary B-tree indexes.

column1: Why does ClickHouse not need a separate heap-fetch step like Postgres' Bitmap Heap Scan?
column2: ClickHouse data is clustered: the rows physically are stored sorted by the ORDER BY key, so the index points straight into the sorted column files. Postgres' B-tree is separate from the heap, so it must do an extra hop to fetch the row bodies.
